q: What is the software development life cycle (SDLC), start to finish?

It is the path a change takes from idea to running in production and then keeps being looked after. The usual stages: plan and define requirements, design, build (write code), test, release (deploy), and operate and monitor, then feed what you learn back into planning. Teams repeat this loop in small slices (agile) instead of one big pass. Knowing which stage you are in tells you who is responsible and what can go wrong.
waterfall vs agile, feedback loops, definition of done.

A request such as 'let customers download invoices' gets written as a ticket, designed by the developer, coded on a branch, reviewed in a pull request, tested by an automated pipeline and QA, released to production, and watched on a dashboard afterwards.
Walk me through what happens from a feature idea to it being live for users.

1) A product manager writes the requirement with acceptance criteria in a ticket (Jira or similar). 2) The team discusses and estimates it, and a developer picks it up. 3) The developer creates a branch, writes code and tests, and opens a pull request. 4) Teammates review it and an automated pipeline builds and tests it. 5) After approval it is merged into the main branch. 6) The pipeline deploys it to a test or staging environment where QA or the product owner checks it. 7) It is released to production, often gradually or behind a feature flag. 8) The team watches logs, metrics and alerts, and fixes problems fast. Each step is a place where you can ask a useful question.
handoffs, who approves what, where bugs get caught.

If an invoice export breaks only for customers with more than 1,000 orders, that is caught most cheaply by a test in step 3, less cheaply in staging, and most expensively by an angry customer in production.
Who does what on a typical engineering team?

Product manager: decides what and why and writes requirements. Engineers (frontend, backend, full-stack): build it. Tech lead or architect: guides design and quality. QA or test engineers: verify it works, often with automation. DevOps or platform engineers: build and run the pipelines and infrastructure. SRE: keep production reliable. Engineering manager: people and delivery. Designers and data people join as needed. Small startups blend these roles, so one person may do several.
DevOps, SRE, QA, tech lead, startup vs enterprise differences.
In a startup the developer who writes the code may also set up the pipeline and be on call; in a large company those are three different teams.
How do agile, scrum and kanban work in practice?

Agile means delivering in small increments and adapting to feedback. Scrum organises work into fixed sprints (often two weeks) with sprint planning, a daily stand-up, a sprint review (demo) and a retrospective, plus a backlog the product owner orders. Kanban skips sprints and limits work in progress on a board of columns. Most teams use a blend. As a PM, your main job inside this is a clear, prioritised backlog and well-written tickets.
backlog, sprint, stand-up, retrospective, story points, velocity.
A two-week sprint might include six tickets; if one slips, the team discusses why in the retrospective instead of hiding it.
What makes a good ticket (user story), acceptance criteria, definition of ready and definition of done?

A good ticket states the user, the need and the outcome, with acceptance criteria that are specific and testable ('given X, when Y, then Z'). Definition of ready: the ticket is clear enough to start (scope, designs, dependencies known). Definition of done: the team's shared checklist for finished work, usually code reviewed, tests passing, deployed to the agreed environment and documented. Vague tickets cause rework, so write what 'done' looks like.
user story format, edge cases, non-goals.
Weak: 'Add search'. Better: 'As a support agent I can search orders by email; results show within 2 seconds for up to 10,000 orders; an unknown email shows a clear empty state'.
What are dev, test, staging and production environments, and why do they exist?

Each environment is a separate copy of the application. Development is where engineers build and try things. Test or QA is where testers verify features. Staging mirrors production as closely as possible for final checks, sometimes called UAT when business users sign off. Production is the live system with real users and real data. Code moves forward through them so mistakes are caught where they are cheap. Differences between environments (data, configuration, scale) are a classic source of 'it worked on my machine' bugs.
UAT, environment parity, configuration per environment, test data.
A feature passes in staging with 50 test orders but is slow in production with 5 million, because the environments were not the same size.
How do the frontend, backend, database and APIs fit together?

The frontend is what users see and click (a website or mobile app). It talks over the network to the backend, which holds the business rules, using APIs. The backend reads and writes a database where data is stored. Other services (payments, email, AI models) are reached through their own APIs. A button click becomes a request to an API endpoint, the backend validates it, applies the business logic, uses the database, and returns a response that the frontend displays.
client-server, request/response, endpoint, third-party APIs.
Clicking 'Place order' sends a request to a create-order endpoint; the backend checks stock, saves the order, charges the card through a payment API and returns a confirmation.
What is a REST API, and what should I know about HTTP methods and status codes?

A REST API exposes resources at URLs and uses HTTP methods: GET reads, POST creates, PUT or PATCH updates, DELETE removes. Responses carry status codes: 2xx success (200 OK, 201 Created), 4xx the caller's mistake (400 bad request, 401 not signed in, 403 not allowed, 404 not found, 429 too many requests), 5xx the server's fault (500, 503). Reviewers check that endpoints validate input, return the right codes, are secured, and do not break existing callers.
JSON, endpoints, idempotency, API versioning, authentication vs authorization.
GET /orders/42 returns that order; GET /orders/9999999 should return 404, not 500 and not an empty 200.
Monolith or microservices: what is the difference and the trade-off?

A monolith is one deployable application containing all features; it is simpler to build, test and run, but a change anywhere means redeploying everything and large teams can step on each other. Microservices split the system into many small services that talk over the network; teams can deploy independently and scale parts separately, at the cost of more complexity (networking, monitoring, data consistency, versioning). Many teams start with a well-organised monolith and split later only where needed.
modular monolith, service boundaries, distributed systems costs.
A startup with six engineers usually ships faster with one codebase than with fifteen microservices.
What should a non-engineer know about databases, migrations and indexes?

Relational databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL) store data in tables with strict structure and are queried with SQL; NoSQL stores (MongoDB, DynamoDB, Redis) trade structure for flexibility or speed. A schema migration is a versioned script that changes the database structure (add a column, create a table) and is run during deployment; risky migrations lock tables or lose data, so they get careful review. An index is a lookup structure that makes certain queries fast but slows writes slightly. Always ask: is this change reversible, and what happens on a very large table?
primary key, foreign key, transaction, ORM, backups.
Adding a column with a default value to a table of 200 million rows can lock it for minutes in some databases, so teams plan such migrations carefully.
How do version numbers, releases and changelogs work?

Semantic versioning writes versions as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: patch for bug fixes, minor for backward-compatible features, major for breaking changes (for example 2.4.1). A release is a tagged, deployable snapshot of the code. A changelog or release notes lists what changed for users. Apps deployed continuously may not show version numbers, but libraries, APIs and mobile apps depend on them.
tags, breaking changes, deprecation, hotfix.
Going from 1.8.3 to 2.0.0 tells every user of a library that something may stop working without code changes on their side.
What are feature flags, and why do teams use them?

A feature flag is a switch in code or configuration that turns a feature on or off without redeploying. Teams use them to merge unfinished work safely, release to a small percentage of users first, run experiments, and turn a problem feature off instantly. The cost: flags add branches to code and must be cleaned up when no longer needed.
gradual rollout, kill switch, A/B tests, flag clean-up.
A new checkout is released to 5% of users; when errors rise, the team switches the flag off in seconds instead of rolling back the whole release.
What is technical debt, and how should a product manager think about it?

Technical debt is the future cost created by shortcuts in code or design: it works now but makes later changes slower and riskier. Some debt is a sensible trade-off to ship fast; unmanaged debt slows every feature and causes incidents. Refactoring is cleaning up code without changing behaviour. A PM helps by making room for debt work, asking engineers to explain the cost of postponing it in plain terms, and not treating all clean-up as optional.
refactoring, code smells, rewrite risk.
'This module has no tests and three copies of the pricing logic' means every price change takes a week and risks a wrong charge.
What are non-functional requirements, and which ones should I ask about?

They describe how well the system works rather than what it does: performance (response time), scalability (more users or data), reliability and availability (uptime), security and privacy, observability, maintainability, accessibility, cost and compliance. Product requirements that skip them cause production problems. Ask for numbers: 'under 2 seconds for 95% of requests', 'survives one server failing', 'personal data encrypted'.
SLA, SLO, latency, throughput, compliance.
A report page that is fine with 100 rows and times out with 100,000 meets the functional requirement but fails the non-functional one.
How should engineers and product managers hand work off and collaborate day to day?

Write clear tickets with acceptance criteria and edge cases, attach designs and examples, be available for questions, review the work in a demo or staging environment against the criteria, and avoid changing scope mid-sprint without discussing the cost. Ask engineers for options and trade-offs, not only dates. Respect that estimates are uncertainty, not promises, and that every added requirement affects testing, deployment and support.
scope creep, demos, estimates, trade-offs.
Instead of 'Can you add this by Friday?' ask 'What is the smallest version we could ship by Friday and what would we skip?'.
Why do dependencies, open-source licences and software supply chain security matter?

Modern applications are mostly third-party packages. Each dependency can carry known vulnerabilities (tracked as CVEs), licence obligations, or abandonment risk. A software bill of materials (SBOM) lists the components in a build so that, when a vulnerability is announced, you can quickly find where you are exposed. Review dependency changes in pull requests: is the package maintained, widely used, appropriately licensed, and free of known issues.
SBOM, CVE, licences, typosquatting, lock files.
A pull request that adds a small, little-known package for one helper function is a flag worth asking about; a built-in or well-known library may do the same job.
What documentation do engineering teams keep, and why?

A README explains what a project is and how to run it; API docs explain how to call it; architecture decision records (ADRs) capture why a choice was made; runbooks list steps to handle operational problems; and the pull request description records the reason for each change. Good documentation saves new teammates days and helps during incidents at 2 a.m.
ADR, runbook, onboarding, comments vs docs.
A runbook for 'payment service errors' might say: check the dashboard, check the provider status page, restart the worker, and escalate to this person if it persists after 15 minutes.
What is Git, and how is it different from GitHub or GitLab?

Git is a version-control tool that tracks every change to files, lets many people work in parallel, and lets you go back in time. GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket are websites that host Git repositories and add collaboration features: pull requests, issues, code review, permissions and automation. Git runs on your computer; the hosting service is the shared place the team pushes to.
repository, remote, clone, origin.
Two developers can edit the same project at once; Git records both histories and helps combine them, and GitHub is where the team compares and approves the result.
Explain commits, branches and merging in plain English.

A commit is a saved snapshot of changes with a message. A branch is a separate line of work so you can change code without touching the main version. Merging brings a branch's commits back into another branch, usually main. The main branch is meant to stay working; new work happens on feature branches that are merged only after review and checks.
main branch, HEAD, history, commit messages.
A developer creates a branch 'add-invoice-export', makes five commits, and opens a pull request to merge it into main.
What is a pull request (PR) or merge request (MR), and why does it exist?

A pull request (GitHub) or merge request (GitLab) is a proposal to merge one branch into another. It shows the exact changes (the diff), a description, discussion comments, and the results of automated checks, and it needs approval before merging. It exists so that at least one other person reviews every change, tests run before code reaches main, and there is a record of what changed and why.
diff, reviewers, approvals, status checks.
Instead of a developer pushing straight to main, they open a PR; two teammates comment, the tests run, and only then is it merged.
What does a good PR description look like?

It says why the change exists (link to the ticket), what changed in a few lines, how it was tested, what is risky or needs attention (migrations, config changes), and screenshots for UI changes. A good description lets a reviewer, or a PM, understand the change without reading every line first.
PR templates, linking tickets, test plan, rollback plan.
'Fixes ORD-123. Adds invoice CSV export. Tested with 10 and 10,000 orders. Adds a new database index (migration included). Rollback: revert and drop index.'
What is the lifecycle of a pull request?

Open (or draft) the PR, automated checks run, reviewers comment, the author pushes more commits to address comments, reviewers approve, all checks are green, and then the PR is merged (often triggering deployment). Branch protection rules usually require approvals and passing checks before the merge button works. Long-lived PRs become painful because main keeps changing, so small, quick PRs are preferred.
draft PR, requested changes, approvals, stale PRs.
A PR opened on Monday with 15 files and 1,200 changed lines might sit for days; splitting it into three smaller PRs usually gets reviewed the same afternoon.
Which branching strategies do teams use: trunk-based development, GitHub Flow and Git Flow?

Trunk-based development: everyone merges small changes to main frequently, hiding unfinished work behind feature flags. GitHub Flow: short-lived feature branches, PR, merge to main, deploy. Git Flow: separate develop, release and hotfix branches, heavier but used for scheduled releases and mobile apps. Pick based on release style; many modern teams prefer short-lived branches.
release branches, hotfix branches, long-lived branches.
A web team deploying daily often uses short branches off main; a team shipping a mobile app monthly may keep a release branch for stabilising each version.
What is the difference between merge, squash and rebase?

Merge commit: joins the branch and keeps all its commits plus a merge commit. Squash merge: combines all the branch's commits into one tidy commit on main. Rebase: replays your commits on top of the latest main to create a straight history. Teams choose one convention; squash merge is common for keeping main readable. Rewriting shared history (rebasing or force-pushing a branch others use) is risky.
linear history, force push, commit hygiene.
A branch with commits named 'wip', 'fix', 'fix again' is squashed into one commit 'Add invoice export (ORD-123)'.
What is a merge conflict, and how is it resolved?

A conflict happens when two branches changed the same lines and Git cannot decide which to keep. The developer opens the file, sees both versions marked, chooses or combines them, tests, and commits the result. Conflicts are normal; frequent small merges keep them small. A wrongly resolved conflict can silently break behaviour, so tests and review still matter.
conflict markers, rebase conflicts, merge tools.
Two people change the tax-rate function the same day; whoever merges second sees the conflict and must combine both changes carefully.
What are branch protection, required checks and CODEOWNERS?

Branch protection rules stop direct pushes to main and require things before merging: a minimum number of approvals, passing automated checks, up-to-date branch, and sometimes signed commits. A CODEOWNERS file names the people or teams who must approve changes to certain folders, such as security or payments code. Together they enforce the review process automatically.
required reviewers, status checks, signed commits.
Changes under /payments automatically request review from the payments team, and the merge button stays disabled until they approve and tests pass.
Which Git commands should a non-engineer recognise?

git clone (copy a repository), git status (what changed), git add and git commit (save a snapshot), git push and git pull (send and fetch changes), git branch and git switch or checkout (work with branches), git diff (see changes), git log (history), git stash (set work aside), git revert (undo a commit safely by adding a new one), git cherry-pick (copy one commit to another branch), git reset (move history, can lose work). Confirm exact options in the current Git documentation before running destructive commands.
reading git log, undoing mistakes safely, destructive commands.
'git revert abc123' creates a new commit that undoes commit abc123, which is safe on a shared branch; 'git reset --hard' can discard work and should be used with care.
Why must secrets never be committed, and what is .gitignore for?

Once a password, API key or token is committed it lives in the repository history and may be copied, so it must be treated as leaked and rotated, even if the line is deleted later. Keep secrets in environment variables or a secrets manager. A .gitignore file lists files Git should not track, such as local configuration, logs and build output. Secret-scanning tools can block pushes that contain keys.
rotating keys, secret scanning, environment variables.
A developer commits a .env file with a cloud key; the key must be revoked and replaced, since removing the file does not erase it from history.
What do small PRs, draft PRs and review etiquette mean in practice?

Small, focused PRs get faster, better reviews and are easier to revert. A draft PR signals work in progress and invites early feedback. Good etiquette: describe the change, review promptly, comment on code not people, mark minor remarks as nits, explain why, and say what is blocking approval.
nit, LGTM, blocking comments, review turnaround.
A comment such as 'nit: rename x to order_count' is a suggestion; 'blocking: this query is built from user input' must be fixed before merge.
How does forking and contributing to open-source projects work?

In open source you fork (copy) the repository to your account, create a branch, make a change, push it, and open a pull request to the original project, where maintainers review it. Good first contributions are documentation fixes and small bugs. Reading the CONTRIBUTING file and past PRs shows the project's standards.
upstream, maintainers, issues, good first issue.
Fixing a typo in a project's README is a safe way to practise the full fork, branch, PR cycle.

s.t: A review method you can use on any pull request
q: How do I review a pull request step by step?

1) Read the ticket and PR description: what is this supposed to do and why? 2) Scan the file list and structure: which layers and folders changed, is the size sensible? 3) Read the tests first: do they describe the intended behaviour? 4) Read the diff top-down, looking for risks (see the checklist) rather than style trivia. 5) Check the automated results (build, tests, lint, security scan). 6) Try it if you can (preview environment or screenshots). 7) Leave clear comments, labelled as blocking or nit, and give an overall verdict: approve, comment, or request changes.
review order, verdicts, preview environments.

For an 'export invoices' PR: read the ticket, see that the tests cover empty, small and huge exports, spot that one query runs inside a loop, and comment 'blocking: this will make one database call per invoice'.
Which review framework should I use so I do not freeze or get lost?

Start broad, then go narrow. First an architectural scan: the file structure and layers (for example routes, controllers, services, repositories, models), and whether the change lives in the right layer. Then the three things anyone can spot quickly: logging, error handling, and hard-coded values. Then deeper risks: resource handling, transactions, validation, security, performance, duplication, tests, and scalability. Do not start by arguing about loops and Big-O; most business code cares more about correctness, safety and clarity.
broad-to-narrow review, risk-based review.
Open the repo, notice there is a service layer and a repository layer, then check whether the service file contains database code. If it does, that is the first architecture comment.
What can a product manager or non-coder usefully check in a PR?

A lot. Does the change match the ticket and acceptance criteria? Are edge cases handled (empty, huge, invalid, duplicate)? Are there tests and do their names describe the behaviour? Is anything user-visible (text, error messages, permissions) wrong? Are logging, error handling and hard-coded values sensible? Does the PR description explain risks and rollout? Does it change an API or data in a way that could break users? Ask questions where you do not understand; a good question is a valid review comment.
asking good questions, acceptance criteria check, risk spotting.
'What happens if the customer has no email address? The ticket says reminders are sent by email.' often finds a real bug that a code-focused reviewer missed.
What are the three issues anyone can spot in seconds: logging, error handling, hard-coded values?

Scroll the file and look for: (1) logging: if the code has none, you cannot debug a failure in production at 2 a.m.; (2) error handling: no try/except around things that can fail (database, network, parsing), or errors swallowed silently; (3) hard-coded values: strings like 'delivered' or numbers like 30 scattered through code instead of named constants, enums or configuration. They are cheap to spot and test whether you think about production.
magic strings, constants, enums, configuration.
A status written as the text 'cancelled' in five places breaks silently the day one spelling changes; a single OrderStatus constant avoids that.
Why does logging matter, and what is good logging?

Logs are the main record of what the program did. Good logging uses levels (debug, info, warning, error), includes context such as an order ID or request ID, records failures with the error details, avoids sensitive data (passwords, card numbers, personal data), and is structured so tools can search it. Not enough logging makes incidents slow to diagnose; too much costs money and hides the signal.
log levels, correlation IDs, structured logs, PII in logs.
'Order creation failed' is weak; 'create_order failed order_id=123 customer=42 reason=payment_declined' tells you where to look.
How should errors and exceptions be handled?

Anticipate what can fail, catch specific errors where you can respond usefully, clean up resources, log the details, and return a clear message or status instead of crashing or hiding the problem. Avoid catching everything and doing nothing (a swallowed error), and avoid leaking internal details to users. Decide what should be retried, what should be rolled back, and what should be reported.
try/except/finally, retries, timeouts, fail fast, error messages.
If a payment call times out, the code should not mark the order paid; it should log the timeout, leave the order pending, and let a retry or a person resolve it.
Why are hard-coded values, magic numbers and secrets in code a problem?

Repeated literal values are easy to mistype and hard to change. Magic numbers hide meaning (what is 86400?). Configuration that differs by environment (URLs, limits) belongs in config. Secrets must never be in code. Prefer named constants, enums, and configuration files or environment variables, which also make tests easier.
enums, constants, config, environment variables.
Replace if status == 'delivered' with if status == OrderStatus.DELIVERED so a typo becomes an error that tools catch.
What is layered architecture (MVC, controller, service, repository), and what belongs in each layer?

Applications are split so each part has one job. Routes or controllers receive requests and map endpoints to handlers, with input validation and HTTP concerns. The service layer holds business rules. The repository (data access) layer talks to the database. Models describe the data. A review smell: database queries or HTTP details inside business logic, or business rules inside controllers. Separation makes code easier to test, change and reuse. Exact naming varies by framework and team.
separation of concerns, MVC, repository pattern, domain logic.
If create_order in the service layer opens a database connection and writes SQL, flag it: that belongs in the repository, so the business rule can be tested without a database.
What is resource management, and what does 'use a context manager' mean?

Resources such as database connections, files and network sockets must be released after use; leaking them eventually exhausts the pool and crashes the service. Close them in a finally block or, better in Python, use a context manager (the with statement), which guarantees clean-up even when an error occurs. Also create expensive objects once (for example in initialisation or a connection pool) rather than on every call.
connection pooling, finally, with statement, leaks.
A function that opens a new database connection on every call and never closes it works in a demo and brings production down after a few thousand requests.
What is a database transaction, and why do 'commit and rollback' matter in review?

A transaction groups several database steps so they succeed or fail together (all or nothing). If an order row is saved but inserting its items fails, without rollback the database is left inconsistent. Review for: related writes inside one transaction, a commit only on success, a rollback on error, and no long-running work inside a transaction. This is a favourite thing for reviewers to check.
atomicity, ACID, rollback, consistency, partial writes.
Charging the card and creating the order are two steps; if the second fails after the first succeeds, the customer is charged for nothing unless the failure is handled.
What input validation should I look for, and where does it belong?

Ask: what if a required field is missing, empty, too long, the wrong type, negative, duplicated, or in an unexpected format? Validate at the boundary (the API layer) so bad data never reaches business logic or the database, and enforce critical rules again in the data layer where needed. Never trust input from users, other services or files.
sanitising, schema validation, boundary conditions, defensive coding.
An order with quantity -5 or an email of 'abc' should be rejected with a clear error, not stored or processed.
What is SQL injection, and how do you spot it?

SQL injection happens when user input is pasted into a SQL string, letting an attacker change the query and read or alter data. Spot it where a query is built with string concatenation or formatting using a variable that comes from a request. The fix is parameterised queries (placeholders) or a safe ORM, never string building. It is a standard security finding.
parameterised queries, ORM, OWASP, input sanitisation.
A query written as 'SELECT ... WHERE status = ' plus the status text is risky; sending status as "x' OR '1'='1" returns rows the caller should never see.
What is the N+1 query problem?

N+1 happens when code runs one query to get a list of N items and then one extra query for each item, so 1,000 orders cause 1,001 database calls. It is fast in tests with five rows and slow in production. Spot a database call or commit inside a loop. Fix by fetching everything in one query (a join or an IN list) or in batches.
batching, joins, eager loading, ORM pitfalls.
Looping over 1,000 orders and calling the database to fetch each order's items takes 1,001 calls; one query that fetches all items for those order IDs takes 2.
How do I check for duplication, reusability and readability?

Look for the same block of code repeated (extract a function), functions that do too many things, vague names, deep nesting, and huge files. AI tools in particular tend to rewrite similar helpers instead of reusing the ones that already exist in a large codebase. Ask whether a new person could understand it in a few minutes. Do not demand perfection; focus on things that will hurt later.
DRY, single responsibility, naming, code smells.
Three functions each opening their own database connection with identical code should share one helper or be moved into initialisation.
How do I judge performance in review without over-focusing on Big-O?

Do not start with 'this is O(n squared)'. First ask what the realistic data size is. Then look for expensive patterns that really bite: queries in loops, missing indexes on large tables, loading everything into memory, calling slow services repeatedly without caching, and no pagination. Fix what matters for real volumes; a nested loop over ten items is fine.
pagination, caching, indexes, premature optimisation.
A nested loop over 20 items is harmless; a list endpoint that returns all 2 million rows without pagination is not.
What security issues should every reviewer look for?

Secrets in code; user input used in queries, shell commands or file paths without checks; missing authentication or authorisation (can user A read user B's data?); sensitive data in logs or error messages; weak or missing encryption; unsafe handling of uploaded files; overly broad permissions; and new dependencies with known vulnerabilities. The OWASP Top 10 is a good checklist; confirm the current edition on the OWASP site.
authentication vs authorisation, OWASP Top 10, least privilege, IDOR.
An endpoint GET /invoices/123 that returns the invoice without checking that it belongs to the signed-in user lets anyone read anyone's invoice by changing the number.
What are race conditions and idempotency, and why do reviewers care?

A race condition is when the result depends on the timing of two actions, such as two requests buying the last item at once. Idempotency means doing the same operation twice has the same effect as doing it once, which is vital for payments and retries. Reviewers ask: what if this runs twice, or two users do it at the same time? Typical fixes are database constraints, locks, and idempotency keys.
double submit, retries, locks, unique constraints.
If a user double-clicks 'Pay' and the code is not idempotent, they might be charged twice; an idempotency key makes the second request return the first result.
How do I review tests and testability?

Check that tests exist for the new behaviour, that they cover failure and edge cases, not only the happy path, and that they would actually fail if the code were wrong (assertions that check something). Watch for tests that only mirror the implementation, excessive mocking that proves nothing, and flaky tests. Code that is hard to test is often badly structured. Huge volumes of generated tests are not the same as meaningful tests.
assertions, mocks, edge cases, flaky tests, coverage.
A test that calls create_order and asserts only that no exception occurred does not prove the order was saved correctly.
How do I review API changes, database migrations and configuration changes?

API: could any existing caller break (removed or renamed fields, changed status codes, new required inputs)? Is it versioned and documented? Database migration: is it reversible, safe on a large table, and compatible with the code that is running during deployment? Configuration and infrastructure: are values right per environment, are secrets handled safely, are permissions minimal? Ask about rollout and rollback for each.
backward compatibility, expand and contract migrations, infrastructure as code.
Renaming the JSON field 'amount' to 'total' will silently break every mobile app version that still reads 'amount'.
How do I review a new dependency or library?

Ask whether it is needed or whether the standard library or an existing dependency already covers it; whether it is actively maintained and widely used; its licence; known vulnerabilities; and its size and transitive dependencies. A lock file change shows exactly what versions were added. Check the package name carefully for typosquatting.
transitive dependencies, licences, lock files, typosquatting.
A PR adds a package with 40 stars and no updates in three years just to format dates; suggest using the standard library or the date library the project already has.
How do I write good review comments and give feedback kindly?

Be specific and kind: say what you see, why it matters, and a suggested fix. Separate blocking issues from nits and questions. Ask 'what happens if...?' instead of accusing. Praise good work. Focus on the code, not the person. Avoid style battles that a formatter or linter should settle. If you are unsure, say so and ask.
nit, blocking, suggestion, praise, tone.
Weak: 'This is wrong.' Better: 'Blocking: this builds SQL from the status parameter, which allows injection. Suggest using a parameterised query, e.g. ...'.
How should I triage review findings by severity?

Blocking (must fix): security holes, data loss or corruption, broken behaviour, breaking changes without a plan. Should fix: missing tests, poor error handling, performance issues on realistic data, clear duplication. Nice to have: naming, style, small refactors. Mark each so the author knows what stops the merge. Too many nits hides the important comments.
priorities, must/should/could, review noise.
SQL injection and a missing rollback are blocking; renaming a variable is a nit.
How do I receive review comments on my own work?

Assume good intent, read each comment, reply with a fix or a reason, thank the reviewer, and do not take it personally. Ask for clarification if you disagree or do not understand. Group your fixes in new commits, re-request review, and learn the team's recurring comments to avoid them next time.
If a reviewer says 'this will not scale', reply with the data size you expect and ask what threshold worries them, then agree on the fix.
What are the typical mistakes in AI-generated code, and what should I watch for?

Common issues: invented or outdated function names and library options (hallucinated APIs); duplicating helpers instead of reusing existing ones in a big codebase; missing logging or weak error handling; incomplete transaction handling; confident but wrong edge-case behaviour; over-engineering; insecure defaults (string-built SQL, broad permissions, secrets in code); and very large volumes of tests that do not assert meaningful behaviour. It is fast but not self-verifying, so the reviewer is the safeguard.
hallucinated APIs, over-engineering, shallow tests, copy-paste duplication.
An AI-written function calls a library method that does not exist in the version you use; the code looks plausible but fails when run. Always run it and check the documentation.
How do I verify that code written by an AI agent is correct, not just plausible?

Run it: the tests, the build and the application. Read the diff against the ticket, not against the AI's summary. Check that every new function and library call really exists in your versions. Test edge cases yourself, look at what changed outside the stated scope, review dependencies it added, and compare against how the rest of the codebase does the same thing. Ask the AI to explain risky parts and list assumptions, then verify the claims.
running code, scope creep in diffs, assumptions, reading the diff.
An agent was asked to fix a bug in one function and also rewrote three unrelated files; the extra changes are the first thing to question.
How can I use AI to help me review, without trusting it blindly?

Ask an AI to summarise the PR, list risks against a checklist (security, transactions, validation, performance, tests), and suggest questions to ask the author. Then verify each claim yourself in the code. Use a second tool or a fresh session for a second opinion, and never approve based only on what an AI said. AI review is an assistant for coverage, not an authority.
review prompts, second opinions, verification.
Prompt: 'Review this diff as a senior backend engineer. List issues under: security, data integrity, error handling, performance, tests. Quote the line for each.' Then open each line and confirm.
What guardrails help when AI agents write code on a team?

Require pull requests and human review for agent changes, keep branch protection and required checks, run tests, linting and security scans automatically, give the agent narrow scope and permissions, never give it production secrets, keep changes small, record which changes were AI-assisted if the team wants that, and keep a clear owner for every change.
least privilege, scoped tasks, CI gates, ownership.
An agent can open PRs but cannot merge to main or deploy; a human approves after the pipeline passes.
How should I answer 'review this code' in an interview when I am new to engineering?

Stay calm and be honest about your level while showing a method. Say what you will do: 'I will scan the structure first, then check logging, error handling and hard-coded values, then data handling, security and tests.' Narrate what you see in plain language, ask clarifying questions, and prioritise findings by severity. Do not pretend to experience you lack; interviewers value a clear method, sound judgement and honesty about what you would verify with the team. The way to speak credibly is to have really practised: review real pull requests (see the practice plan) and describe those.
framing, prioritisation, honesty, practice.

'I have not run a large production system, but I have reviewed pull requests on open-source projects and my own, and here is how I approach them: ...' is stronger than bluffing and holds up under follow-up questions.
What are CI and CD, and why do teams use them?

Continuous integration (CI) means every change is automatically built and tested as soon as it is pushed, so problems show up in minutes, not weeks. Continuous delivery means the code is always in a releasable state and can be deployed with one approved step; continuous deployment goes further and releases automatically when checks pass. Together they replace manual, error-prone releases with a repeatable pipeline.
automation, fast feedback, release frequency.
A developer pushes a branch; within ten minutes the pipeline reports that the build passes but two tests fail, before any human reviews the code.
What stages does a typical CI/CD pipeline have?

Common stages: check out the code; install dependencies; lint and format checks; build; unit tests; integration tests; security scans (dependencies, static analysis, secrets); package the application (often as a Docker image) and store it as an artifact; deploy to a test or staging environment; run smoke or end-to-end tests; then, after approval or automatically, deploy to production and verify. A failure at any stage stops the pipeline and blocks the merge or release.
build artifact, smoke test, quality gates, approvals.
A pull request fails at the lint stage because of unused imports; the developer fixes it in two minutes instead of a reviewer pointing it out.
What are Jenkins, GitHub Actions and GitLab CI, and how do they differ?

They are tools that run pipelines. Jenkins is a long-established, self-hosted automation server configured with a Jenkinsfile and plugins, flexible but you maintain it. GitHub Actions runs workflows defined in YAML files in the repository and is built into GitHub. GitLab CI works the same way using a .gitlab-ci.yml file inside GitLab. The concepts are the same: triggers, jobs, steps, environments and secrets; the syntax differs.
YAML, runners, triggers, secrets in pipelines.
A workflow file might say: on every pull request, run the tests; on merge to main, build the image and deploy to staging.
What are build artifacts, Docker images and container registries?

A build artifact is the packaged output of a build that gets deployed. A Docker image packages the application with everything it needs to run, and a container is a running instance of an image, so it behaves the same on a laptop, in testing and in production. Images are stored in a container registry and referenced by tag. Reviewers look at Dockerfiles for pinned versions, unnecessary files, running as root, and secrets baked into images.
Dockerfile, image tags, registry, containers vs virtual machines.
Deploying means telling the platform to run image 'orders-api:1.14.2' from the registry; rolling back means running 1.14.1 again.
What is Kubernetes, in one answer?

Kubernetes is a system that runs and manages many containers across many machines: it starts them, restarts failed ones, scales them up and down, spreads traffic, and rolls out new versions gradually. Teams describe the desired state in configuration files and Kubernetes works to keep reality matching it. You do not need to operate it to review work, but you should recognise the words: pod, deployment, service, cluster, namespace.
pods, deployments, scaling, health checks.
If a container crashes, Kubernetes notices and starts a new one automatically; if traffic doubles it can add copies.
What is the test pyramid, and what kinds of tests exist?

Many fast unit tests (one function or class), fewer integration tests (parts working together, such as code plus database), and a few slow end-to-end tests (the whole system through the user interface or API). Others: smoke tests (is it alive), regression tests (did an old bug come back), performance and load tests, security tests, and acceptance tests against requirements. Cheap tests at the bottom catch most problems quickly.
unit, integration, end-to-end, regression, smoke, load tests.
A unit test checks that the discount function returns 90 for 100 with 10% off; an end-to-end test logs in, adds an item and pays.
Who tests what: developers, QA, UAT and automation?

Developers write unit and integration tests for their code. QA engineers design test strategies, explore edge cases, and build automated suites. UAT (user acceptance testing) is where the business or customer confirms the feature meets the need, often in staging. Automation runs in the pipeline for every change; manual or exploratory testing finds the surprises. Quality is a shared responsibility, not just QA's.
exploratory testing, acceptance testing, test plans, bug reports.
The pipeline runs 2,000 automated tests in 8 minutes; QA spends the sprint trying unusual sequences such as cancelling an order halfway through payment.
What does code coverage tell you, and what does it not?

Coverage is the percentage of lines or branches executed by tests. Low coverage means large parts are untested, but high coverage does not prove good tests: a test can run a line without checking anything. Use it as a warning light and look at whether the important and risky paths are meaningfully tested.
line vs branch coverage, mutation testing, coverage thresholds.
100% coverage with tests that never assert anything would still miss every bug.
What are linting, formatting, static analysis and SAST?

A formatter makes code style consistent automatically. A linter flags likely mistakes and style issues. Static analysis inspects code without running it for bugs, and SAST (static application security testing) specifically looks for security flaws such as injection or hard-coded secrets. Running these in the pipeline removes boring comments from human review so people can focus on design and risk.
type checking, SonarQube-style tools, pre-commit hooks.
A pipeline step fails because a linter found an unused variable and a scanner found an API key in a file, before a human opens the PR.
How are dependency vulnerabilities and SBOMs checked in a pipeline?

Tools scan the project's dependencies against databases of known vulnerabilities (CVEs) and report severity and available fixes; policies can fail the build above a threshold. An SBOM (software bill of materials) lists every component in a build, so that when a new vulnerability appears you can see immediately which applications are affected. Also scan container images and licences. A firewall for dependencies can block risky packages before they enter the build.
CVE, severity, remediation, licence policy, supply chain.
When a critical vulnerability in a popular logging library is announced, teams with SBOMs can list affected services in minutes instead of days.
How are configuration and secrets managed across environments?

Code stays the same; configuration changes per environment through environment variables or config files kept outside the code. Secrets (passwords, tokens, keys) live in a secrets manager or the pipeline's encrypted secret store, are given only to the services that need them, are rotated regularly, and never appear in code, logs or images.
environment variables, secrets manager, rotation, 12-factor config.
The staging environment reads DATABASE_URL pointing at the test database; production reads a different value, with no code change.
What are rolling, blue-green and canary deployments?

Rolling: replace old instances with new ones a few at a time. Blue-green: run the new version (green) next to the old (blue) and switch traffic over at once, switching back if something is wrong. Canary: send a small share of traffic (say 5%) to the new version, watch metrics, and increase gradually. All reduce risk compared with replacing everything at once.
zero-downtime deploys, traffic shifting, health checks.
A canary release sends 5% of users to version 1.15; error rates look normal after an hour, so it goes to 25%, then 100%.
What is a rollback, a hotfix and a revert?

A rollback returns production to the previous working version, usually the fastest response to a bad release. A revert undoes the problem change in the code (a new commit that reverses it). A hotfix is an urgent small fix that skips the normal schedule but should still go through a lighter review and the pipeline. Plan for rollback before you release, especially with database changes.
incident response, forward fix vs rollback, rollback plan.
If version 1.15 causes errors, redeploy 1.14 first to stop the damage; investigate and fix properly afterwards.
What is infrastructure as code?

Infrastructure as code means servers, networks, databases and permissions are defined in version-controlled files (with tools such as Terraform, CloudFormation or Pulumi) and created by running them, so environments are repeatable and changes are reviewed like code. Review these PRs for security groups open to the world, over-broad permissions, missing backups and cost impact.
Terraform, drift, reviewable infrastructure.
A PR that opens a database to 0.0.0.0/0 (the whole internet) should be a blocking comment.
How are database migrations deployed safely?

Migrations are versioned scripts run during deployment. Safe practice: make changes backward compatible so old and new code work during the rollout (add a column before using it; remove it only later), test on production-sized data, take a backup, avoid long locks, and plan how to roll back. Separate risky data changes from application releases when you can.
expand and contract, backfills, locks, backups.
To rename a column safely, add the new column, write to both, copy the old data, switch reads, and only then drop the old column in a later release.
What are logs, metrics and traces (observability), and what do alerts and SLOs add?

Logs are detailed event records; metrics are numbers over time (requests per second, error rate, latency); traces follow one request through many services. Observability means you can understand what is happening inside the system from these signals. Alerts notify people when metrics cross thresholds. An SLO (service level objective) is a target such as 99.9% of requests succeed, and the error budget is how much failure you can tolerate.
dashboards, latency percentiles, error budget, monitoring tools.
A dashboard shows checkout errors rising from 0.1% to 4% after a deploy; the alert fires and the on-call engineer rolls back.
How does incident response work, and what is a postmortem?

When production breaks: detect through alerts, declare an incident and name a lead, stabilise first (rollback, disable the feature flag, add capacity), communicate to stakeholders, then find the root cause and fix it. Afterwards a blameless postmortem records the timeline, the causes, what worked, and follow-up actions with owners. The aim is learning, not blame. On-call engineers carry the pager for their service during their rotation.
on-call, severity levels, blameless culture, root cause analysis.
After an outage caused by a migration, the action items might be: add a check for migration locks in review, and add an alert for slow queries.
What happens, step by step, after I click 'merge' on a pull request?

The change joins the main branch. The pipeline starts: build, run tests, scan, package, and store a versioned image. It then deploys automatically to a test or staging environment and runs smoke tests. Depending on the team, production deployment is automatic, or a person approves it, or it happens on a release schedule, possibly gradual with a feature flag. After release the team watches dashboards and alerts. If something goes wrong, they roll back or turn off the flag.
continuous deployment, approvals, post-deploy verification.
You merge at 11:00; by 11:12 the image is in staging, by 11:30 a canary is serving 5% of production, and at 12:00 it is at 100% with no alerts.
What do release management and change approvals look like in larger companies?

Larger or regulated companies add formal steps: change tickets, release windows, approvals from security or compliance, release notes, and sometimes a change advisory board for risky changes. Startups often release many times a day with only automated checks. Know which model your team uses, and plan requirements around its release rhythm.
change management, release trains, compliance, audit trails.
A bank may deploy only on Tuesday nights after sign-off; a startup may deploy twenty times a day.
What are performance testing and load testing?

Performance tests measure speed and resource use; load tests apply realistic or heavy traffic to see how the system behaves and where it breaks; stress tests push beyond limits. They reveal slow queries, missing indexes, memory leaks and capacity limits before customers do. Run them in an environment that resembles production.
latency percentiles, throughput, bottlenecks, capacity planning.
A load test of 5,000 simultaneous users shows response times jumping from 200 ms to 8 seconds, pointing to a missing database index.
What are flaky tests, and why are they harmful?

A flaky test sometimes passes and sometimes fails with no code change, often because of timing, shared state or external services. They erode trust: people re-run pipelines and ignore real failures. Fix or quarantine them quickly; do not train the team to shrug at red builds.
A test that depends on the current second ticking over passes 99 times and fails once, blocking a release on the hundredth.
Exercise 1: review this create-order function. What would you comment on?

Read it first, then check the findings.
```
class OrderService:
    def create_order(self, customer_email, items):
        conn = get_connection()
        cur = conn.cursor()
        cur.execute("INSERT INTO orders (email, status) VALUES (%s, 'created')", (customer_email,))
        order_id = cur.lastrowid
        for item in items:
            cur.execute("INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, sku, qty) VALUES (%s, %s, %s)",
                        (order_id, item['sku'], item['qty']))
        conn.commit()
        return order_id
```
Findings, roughly by priority. Transactions: if one item insert fails halfway, the order exists without its items and there is no rollback. Resource management: the connection is never closed, and a new one is opened on every call (use a context manager or pool). Error handling: nothing catches database errors. Logging: no record of success or failure. Validation: email or quantity could be missing, empty or negative. Hard-coded value: the status text 'created' should be a constant or enum. Layering: database code sits in the service layer and belongs in a repository. Performance: one insert per item is a mild N+1 pattern; a batch insert is better for big orders.
transactions, resource leaks, layering, validation, logging.
In an interview you would say: 'Before style, the biggest risk is a half-saved order because there is no transaction handling; second is the leaked connection.'
Exercise 2: what is wrong with this count-by-status function?

Try it, then read on.
```
def count_orders(self, status):
    conn = get_connection()
    cur = conn.cursor()
    cur.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status = '" + status + "'")
    return cur.fetchone()[0]
```
The query is built by joining the status text into the SQL, which is a SQL injection vulnerability: a caller could pass text that changes the query. Use a parameterised query: cur.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status = %s", (status,)). Also flag the unclosed connection, no logging or error handling, and that status values should come from a defined list, not free text. The placeholder style (%s or ?) depends on the database driver, so check its documentation.
parameterised queries, validation of allowed values, resource handling.
Comment to leave: 'Blocking: the status value goes straight into the SQL string. Please use a placeholder so the driver escapes it.'
Exercise 3: spot the N+1 query in this order-listing function.

```
def list_orders_with_items(self):
    orders = self.repo.get_all_orders()
    result = []
    for o in orders:
        items = self.repo.get_items_for_order(o.id)
        result.append({'order': o, 'items': items})
    return result
```
The database is called once for the orders and then once per order inside the loop: 1,000 orders cause 1,001 queries. Fix by fetching all items for those order IDs in one query (a join, or an IN list) and grouping them in memory, or by using the ORM's eager-loading feature. Also ask about pagination: returning every order at once will not scale.
batching, joins, pagination.
Say in review: 'This does one query per order. With 1,000 orders that is 1,001 queries; could we fetch the items in one call?'
Exercise 4: what is risky in this endpoint and its config?

```
API_KEY = "sk_live_51Hxxxxxxxxxxxx"

@app.get("/invoices/{invoice_id}")
def get_invoice(invoice_id: int):
    invoice = db.get_invoice(invoice_id)
    print("fetched", invoice)
    return invoice
```
A live-looking secret is committed in code: remove it, rotate the key, and read it from an environment variable or secret store. There is no authentication or authorisation check, so anyone could read any invoice by changing the number. The print statement should be proper logging and it may log sensitive data. A missing invoice probably yields an error or null instead of a clear 404. Security issues are blocking comments.
secrets, authorisation, IDOR, logging of sensitive data, status codes.
Say: 'Blocking: this endpoint returns any invoice to any caller. Please verify the invoice belongs to the signed-in customer.'
Exercise 5: this change was written by an AI agent. What do you check before approving?
hallucinated dependencies, idempotency, timeouts, scope check.
An AI summary can sound right while the code is not; always run it and read the diff, not the summary.
Exercise 6: what would you flag in this Dockerfile and pipeline snippet?

```
FROM python:latest
COPY . /app
ENV DB_PASSWORD=admin123
RUN pip install -r /app/requirements.txt
CMD python /app/main.py
```
The base image uses the latest tag, so builds are not repeatable (pin a version). A password is baked into the image: use runtime secrets. Copying everything may include .git, local config and secrets (use .dockerignore). The container runs as root by default (add a non-root user). Dependencies are installed after copying the source, which breaks build caching. No health check. Dockerfile best practice evolves, so verify against current official guidance.
pinning versions, secrets in images, least privilege.
Comment: 'Blocking: DB_PASSWORD is stored in the image layers and visible to anyone who can pull the image.'
What is a realistic 14-day plan for a non-coder to become comfortable with the engineering workflow?

Days 1-2: create a GitHub account, make a practice repository, learn clone, branch, commit, push, and open and merge your own pull request. Days 3-4: read this bank's lifecycle and Git sections and draw the idea-to-production flow for a product you know. Days 5-7: read five merged pull requests in an active open-source project and write what each one changed and why; then read five open ones and leave one question each (or draft your comments privately). Days 8-9: add a simple automated check to your practice repo with GitHub Actions (run a test or linter) and watch it fail and pass. Days 10-11: do the six code-review exercises, then review a small AI-generated change using the checklist. Days 12-13: study CI/CD, deployment strategies and incidents; read a public postmortem. Day 14: write a one-page review checklist in your own words and do a mock review aloud.
deliberate practice, real artefacts, mock interviews.
By day 14 you should have: a repository with merged PRs, a working pipeline, ten reviewed pull requests, and a checklist you can explain without notes.
How do I practise reviewing without a job or a team?

Use public repositories: browse merged pull requests of popular projects, read the description, the diff and the maintainers' comments, and notice what reviewers ask for. Practise on your own repo by opening a PR for every change and reviewing it the next day with a checklist. Ask an AI to write a deliberately flawed function and find the issues before asking it for the answer, then verify what it says. Pair with a developer friend for 30 minutes and ask them to narrate how they review.
open-source PR reading, self-review, flawed-code exercises, pairing.
Pick a project you use, filter pull requests by 'merged', and read the review comments on three of them each day.
How can I use ShipCode and this app's own repository to practise the real workflow?

If you have access to a repository such as your own copy of a project, do the full cycle for a tiny change: create a branch, edit a text, run the tests, commit with a clear message, open a PR with a proper description, review it as if someone else wrote it, merge it, and watch the deployment and the live site. Then break something on purpose in a branch, see the checks fail, and fix it. This turns the vocabulary into things you have actually done.
branch, PR, checks, deploy, rollback.
Change one sentence on a page, open a PR, wait for the preview deployment, approve, merge, and confirm the live page changed.
How do I talk about my experience truthfully when moving from product to a technical role?

Describe what you really did: the products you owned, the requirements and acceptance criteria you wrote, the PRs and demos you reviewed or tested, the incidents you helped triage, and the hands-on practice you have done since. Say clearly where you are learning. Interviewers for forward-deployed and technical roles probe details, so claimed experience that you cannot defend hurts you; a PM with real review habits, honest depth and fast learning is credible. Build real artefacts (a repo, a pipeline, reviewed PRs) so your examples are true.
honest framing, evidence, learning narrative, projects.

'In my last role I wrote the acceptance criteria, joined the sprint demos and tested builds in staging. Since then I have built and reviewed PRs on my own repo and learned to run a pipeline; here is what I check first...' is accurate and strong.
What is the smallest daily habit that builds this skill?

Read one real pull request a day for fifteen minutes: the description, the diff, the comments and the outcome, and write down one risk you noticed and one thing you did not understand. After a month that is about thirty reviewed changes and a list of concepts to look up.
Keep a notes file: date, repo, PR link, what changed, risks I spotted, terms to learn.

gl: Software development life cycle: the stages a change goes through, from planning and building to testing, releasing and monitoring.
A proposal to merge your changes into the main code. Teammates review it and automated checks run before it is merged.
GitLab's name for a pull request.
The view of exactly which lines were added, changed or removed in a change.
A saved snapshot of changes in Git, with a message saying what changed.
A separate line of work in Git, so changes do not touch the main code until they are merged.
A tool that records every change to files and lets many people work on the same code safely.
Websites that host Git repositories and add pull requests, issues and automation.
The folder of code plus its full change history.
The primary version of the code that is meant to always work.
When two changes touch the same lines and Git cannot decide which to keep, so a person must choose.
Replaying your commits on top of the latest main to keep history in a straight line.
Combining all commits of a branch into one tidy commit when merging.
Copying one specific commit onto another branch.
Undoing a change by adding a new commit that reverses it. Safe on shared branches.
Overwriting the remote branch history. Risky on shared branches.
A pull request marked not ready, to show work in progress and get early feedback.
Reviewer shorthand for 'looks good to me', meaning approval.
A tiny, non-blocking review remark such as a naming suggestion.
A file naming who must approve changes to certain parts of the code.
Rules that stop direct pushes to main and require approvals and passing checks before merging.
Automation that builds and tests every change (CI) and releases it in a repeatable way (CD).
The automated sequence of build, test, scan and deploy steps run for every change.
A long-standing, self-hosted tool for running build and deployment pipelines.
Pipeline tools built into GitHub and GitLab, configured with files in the repository.
The packaged output of a build that gets deployed, such as an image or a file.
A way to package an application with everything it needs so it runs the same everywhere.
A running, isolated instance of a packaged application.
A storage service for container images, where deployments pull them from.
A system that runs, scales and heals many containers across many machines.
A separate running copy of the application: development, test, staging or production.
A near-copy of production used for final checks before release. UAT is user acceptance testing.
The real running system used by real customers.
An urgent small fix released outside the normal schedule.
Returning to the previous working version after a bad release or failed operation.
Releasing a new version to a small share of users first and watching before rolling out wider.
Running the new version beside the old and switching traffic over at once, with an easy switch back.
A switch that turns a feature on or off without redeploying code.
Automatic checks for likely mistakes and style problems in code.
Inspecting code without running it to find bugs and security flaws.
A small, fast test of one function or class.
A test that checks several parts working together, such as code plus a database.
A test that drives the whole system the way a user would.
An old bug or behaviour that comes back after a change.
A quick check that the basics work after a deployment.
The share of code executed by tests. Useful as a warning light, not proof of good tests.
A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails with no code change.
A performance trap where code makes one database call per item in a list instead of one call for all.
An attack where user input changes a database query because it was pasted into the SQL text.
A safe way to run SQL where values are passed separately from the query text.
A group of database steps that all succeed together or all fail together.
Doing an action twice has the same effect as doing it once. Vital for payments and retries.
A bug where the outcome depends on the exact timing of two actions.
A Python feature that guarantees clean-up, such as closing a connection, even when errors happen.
A shared set of reusable database connections, instead of opening a new one each time.
A fixed list of allowed named values, such as order statuses, used instead of loose text.
A literal value in code with no name or explanation, easy to mistype and hard to change.
A way to organise code into separate layers, such as controllers, business logic and data access.
Keeping all database code in one layer so the rest of the code does not touch the database directly.
Future cost created by shortcuts in code or design that make later changes slower and riskier.
Cleaning up code structure without changing what it does.
A sign in the code that something may be wrong, though it is not necessarily a bug.
Don't repeat yourself: put repeated logic in one place.
The defined way one program asks another for data or actions.
A common API style using URLs for things and HTTP methods like GET and POST for actions.
A number in a web response: 2xx success, 4xx caller's mistake, 5xx server's fault.
Checking what you are allowed to do or see once you are known.
A well-known list of the most common web security risks.
A password, token or key that must never be stored in code or logs.
A setting supplied to the program from outside its code, such as a database address.
A package of someone else's code that your application relies on.
Software bill of materials: a list of every component in a build, used to find out quickly what is affected by a new vulnerability.
A public ID for a known security vulnerability.
Version numbers in MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH form: major means breaking changes, minor adds features, patch fixes bugs.
Defining servers, networks and databases in files that are reviewed and run like code.
A versioned script that changes the database structure during deployment.
Being able to understand a running system from its logs, metrics and traces.
Recording what a program did, with levels such as info and error, so failures can be diagnosed.
Numbers tracked over time, such as error rate and response time, shown on dashboards.
A reliability target, such as 99.9% of requests succeed. SLA is the promise made to customers.
The engineer responsible for responding to production problems during their rotation.
A production problem that affects users. A postmortem is the blameless write-up of what happened and what to change.
One application containing all features, deployed as a single unit.
Many small services, each handling one job and talking over the network.
A way of working in short fixed cycles (sprints) with regular planning, check-ins and reviews.
The ordered list of work the team may do.
Specific, testable statements of what must be true for a ticket to count as done.
A function or library an AI invented that does not exist.
A malicious package with a name almost identical to a popular one.
